chief_complaint: painless, progressively enlarging 3 cm lateral neck mass in a heavy smoker with unilateral tonsillar asymmetry concerning for Head & Neck Cancer
hpi_details: 61M heavy smoker and social drinker presents with a 3-month history of a painless, hard lump on the left side of his upper neck just below the jawline that has steadily grown to 3 cm. Denies fever, sore throat, or ear pain. However, upon targeted questioning, admits to mild pain when swallowing solids over the past month, a feeling of a lump stuck in the left side of his throat, and occasional blood streaks in his saliva.

concerns: worried because antibiotic courses from urgent care failed to shrink the lump
expectations: wants CT scan and biopsy to rule out cancer

clinical_knowledge.topic: Metastatic Squamous Cell Carcinoma (Head & Neck, from tonsillar primary) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Metastatic Squamous Cell Carcinoma (Head & Neck, from tonsillar primary) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes prompt tissue diagnosis via fine-needle aspiration, cross-sectional and metabolic staging imaging, and referral to head and neck surgical oncology, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: painless, progressively enlarging 3 cm lateral neck mass in a heavy smoker with unilateral tonsillar asymmetry concerning for Head & Neck Cancer

Key HPI features: 61M heavy smoker and social drinker presents with a 3-month history of a painless, hard lump on the left side of his upper neck just below the jawline that has steadily grown to 3 cm. Denies fever, sore throat, or ear pain. However, upon targeted questioning, admits to mild pain when swallowing solids over the past month, a feeling of a lump stuck in the left side of his throat, and occasional blood streaks in his saliva.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 78, BP 138/84. Neck examination palpates a 3.2 x 2.8 cm hard, non-tender, fixed lymph node in Level II of the left anterior cervical triangle (jugulodigastric chain). Oropharyngeal examination reveals noticeable asymmetry of the tonsillar fossae: the left palatine tonsil is enlarged, indurated, and ulcerated compared to the normal right tonsil. Flexible fiberoptic nasopharyngolaryngoscopy confirms left tonsillar ulceration extending to the base of tongue. CRITICAL ONCOLOGICAL MANDATE: DO NOT PERFORM OPEN EXCISIONAL OR INCISIONAL BIOPSY OF A CERVICAL LYMPH NODE in an adult with suspected head and neck cancer (open neck biopsy disrupts lymphatic planes, causes tumor seeding across the neck, reduces cure rates, and complicates definitive surgical neck dissection).
Relevant background/PMH: Hypertension, 45 pack-year cigarette smoking history, drinks 3-4 beers daily
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Metastatic Squamous Cell Carcinoma (Head & Neck, from tonsillar primary).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Reactive lymphadenitis from infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Failure to shrink with antibiotics — a lump that persists past a course of antibiotics needs biopsy, not another course.
management_principles: Perform STAT Fine-Needle Aspiration (FNA) or Ultrasound-guided Core Needle Biopsy of the left Level II neck mass (which avoids violating neck fascial planes and seeding tumor)
Order Contrast-Enhanced CT and PET-CT of Neck and Chest for complete anatomical and metastatic staging
Refer to Head and Neck Surgical Oncology for Panendoscopy (Direct Laryngoscopy, Bronchoscopy, Esophagoscopy with biopsies of left tonsil primary) under general anesthesia
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 61M high-risk smoker/drinker presenting with a persistent, enlarging, painless lateral neck mass and unilateral odynophagia, representing metastatic squamous cell carcinoma to a cervical lymph node from an occult upper aerodigestive tract primary.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 78, BP 138/84. Neck examination palpates a 3.2 x 2.8 cm hard, non-tender, fixed lymph node in Level II of the left anterior cervical triangle (jugulodigastric chain). Oropharyngeal examination reveals noticeable asymmetry of the tonsillar fossae: the left palatine tonsil is enlarged, indurated, and ulcerated compared to the normal right tonsil. Flexible fiberoptic nasopharyngolaryngoscopy confirms left tonsillar ulceration extending to the base of tongue. CRITICAL ONCOLOGICAL MANDATE: DO NOT PERFORM OPEN EXCISIONAL OR INCISIONAL BIOPSY OF A CERVICAL LYMPH NODE in an adult with suspected head and neck cancer (open neck biopsy disrupts lymphatic planes, causes tumor seeding across the neck, reduces cure rates, and complicates definitive surgical neck dissection).
reference_soap.assessment: Metastatic Squamous Cell Carcinoma to Left Cervical Lymph Node (Level II, cN2a) from Left Palatine Tonsil Primary (Human Papillomavirus p16 status pending vs Tobacco-related SCC).
reference_soap.plan: 1. Perform STAT Fine-Needle Aspiration (FNA) or Ultrasound-guided Core Needle Biopsy of the left Level II neck mass (which avoids violating neck fascial planes and seeding tumor). 2. Order Contrast-Enhanced CT and PET-CT of Neck and Chest for complete anatomical and metastatic staging. 3. Refer to Head and Neck Surgical Oncology for Panendoscopy (Direct Laryngoscopy, Bronchoscopy, Esophagoscopy with biopsies of left tonsil primary) under general anesthesia. Multidisciplinary tumor board coordination for definitive chemoradiotherapy vs transoral robotic surgery (TORS) plus neck dissection.

learning_objectives: Understand the cardinal oncological rule: an asymmetric, hard, painless lateral neck mass in an adult >40 (especially smokers/drinkers) is metastatic squamous cell carcinoma from an upper aerodigestive tract primary until proven otherwise

Explain the strict absolute contraindication against open surgical biopsy (excisional or incisional) of a cervical neck mass prior to thorough mucosal evaluation, utilizing Fine-Needle Aspiration (FNA) instead to prevent tumor seeding and lymphatic disruption
Correlate unilateral tonsillar enlargement/ulceration or base-of-tongue induration with oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (p16+ HPV-related vs tobacco/alcohol-related)
Outline diagnostic staging steps including Panendoscopy (laryngoscopy/bronchoscopy/esophagoscopy) and PET-CT prior to definitive multidisciplinary treatment

teaching.diagnosis: Metastatic Squamous Cell Carcinoma (Head & Neck, from tonsillar primary)
teaching.one_liner: A painless, hard, enlarging neck lump in a heavy smoker/drinker that hasn't responded to antibiotics — with subtle clues like swallowing pain and blood-streaked saliva — is head and neck cancer until proven otherwise, needing biopsy and staging.
differentials: Branchial cleft cyst (would not be new in a 61-year-old)
red_flags: Failure to shrink with antibiotics — a lump that persists past a course of antibiotics needs biopsy, not another course

must_ask.say: How long has this lump been there, and has it been growing?
Do you have any pain swallowing, or a feeling of something stuck in your throat?
Have you noticed any blood when you spit or in your saliva?
How much have you smoked and how much do you drink?
Did the antibiotics from urgent care help at all?
